title: Discovering Opinion Intervals from Conflicts in Signed Graphs

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.1, Theorem 2.2 (Revised); Introduction 'Our results'; Section 5 Conclusion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 2.2 is labeled '(Revised)' and explicitly states: 'the interval assignments encoding acyclic partitions rely on strict ordering assumptions that do not hold in all interval configurations. Consequently, the proposed reduction does not guarantee an equivalence between acyclic partitions and conflict-free interval representations in G. Therefore, the NP-hardness claim for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION remains open under the current construction, pending a corrected reduction.' Yet the same section immediately lists 'The theorem has several implications... (1) The disagreement version is hard to approximate within any factor. (2) It is not FPT when parameterized by the number of required edge deletions (unless P = NP)... (3) The result holds even when restricted to graphs... where G^+ is a chordless cycle' as though the theorem were established. The Introduction asserts 'we show that BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION is NP-hard even when the graph G^+ = (V, E^+) induced by the positive edges forms a cycle' and 'there is no FPT algorithm that is parameterized by the number of required edge removals, and that the disagreement version... cannot be approximated within any multiplicative factor.' The Conclusion states 'We gave strong hardness results for incomplete graphs.' The paper simultaneously claims and disclaims its central theoretical contribution; the implications list and the Intro/Conclusion overclaim are unsupported once the NP-hardness claim is retracted. Appendix A also still presents a full proof asserting correctness.

The main-text discussion of the PTAS states: 'We attempt to solve the generalized CORRELATION CLUSTERING problem by partitioning V into m based on random sampling but acknowledge that overlapping intervals introduce intricate dependencies making greedy assignments approximate at best. The complexity of enumerating assignments grows exponentially with the number of overlapping cluster combinations, which may be prohibitively large. Due to these challenges, while a PTAS is feasible for limited and well-structured interval overlaps, the general case requires further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods.' This directly contradicts Theorem 2.3, which claims an unconditional PTAS: 'There exists an algorithm that, with probability at least 1 − δ, returns a (1 + ε)-approximate solution for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION when the algorithm can only use k different intervals and it runs in time 2^{O(k^2 log(k/(εδ))/ε^3)} · n.' If the general case requires 'further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods,' the theorem's general guarantee cannot stand as stated; one of the two passages is wrong.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 8 (Appendix C.7), party-affiliation table vs Table 1 |V|=1,480
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 8 reports per-party counts of Bundestag members assigned to each of the 8 intervals. Row sums are LINKE ≈250, GRÜNE ≈400, SPD ≈750, FDP ≈300, CDU/CSU ≈700, AfD ≈200, for a total of ≈2,600 members. However, Table 1 states the Bundestag signed graph has |V| = 1,480 vertices (also consistent with the C.7 statement that 'This left two politicians without any edges, which were thus excluded'), and each vertex is assigned to exactly one interval. The sum of the table (≈2,600) exceeds the stated vertex count by ~76%. Additionally, interval 4 alone holds ≈950 members (650 SPD + 150 GRÜNE + 150 FDP) and interval 5 ≈850, so the two middle intervals alone exceed 1,480. The table is internally inconsistent with the dataset size reported elsewhere.

summary: The paper contains three high-confidence internal inconsistencies (>= 0.85), one of which undermines its central theoretical contribution. (1) Theorem 2.2 '(Revised)' explicitly retracts the claimed NP-hardness of BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION ('the NP-hardness claim ... remains open under the current construction'), yet the Introduction asserts the cycle-hardness result and the no-FPT / no-approximation consequences as established, the immediately following implications list (1)-(3) treats the theorem as proven, Appendix A still presents a correctness proof, and the Conclusion claims 'We gave strong hardness results for incomplete graphs.' The paper simultaneously claims and disclaims its headline hardness result. (2) The Section 2.2 discussion states that a PTAS holds only for 'limited and well-structured interval overlaps' and that 'the general case requires further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods,' directly contradicting Theorem 2.3's unconditional (1+epsilon)-approximation PTAS for all complete graphs with k intervals. (3) Figure 8's party-per-interval table sums to approximately 2,600 Bundestag members, contradicting the stated dataset size of |V| = 1,480 vertices (interval 4 alone holds ~950). Numeric checks that PASS: all eight Table 1 improvement percentages are computed correctly as (best baseline - best of GAIA/VENUS)/best baseline (e.g., BitcoinOTC 40.39%, Bundestag 91.53%); the claimed '38% fewer disagreements on average' matches the 38.8% average of the improvement column; |E+|+|E-|=|E| holds for all eight datasets in Table 2; the Bundestag 0.25% violated-edges figure is consistent with 1,001/397,497 = 0.2518% (Table 4). A minor, non-critical observation: the proof of Lemma B.3 writes E[Y] < (epsilon*delta/(32mk))|V_i|, omitting the factor of k from the union bound over the k intervals; the stated lemma probability 1 - delta/(4m) is nonetheless correct once that union bound is applied, so the proof text is arithmetically slipshod but the lemma stands.
